source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

In the crowded ER, the desk was bustling with activity. Papers were scattered, and forms filled with patient details lay on the surface. Nurses hurried between the bays, their steps steady but purposeful. A doctor, clipboard in hand, moved alongside them, his gaze sharp and intent. The monitors beeped rhythmically, and IV drips hummed softly. A curtain was drawn, dividing a private space where a patient groaned in distress, flanked by a concerned companion. The intercom crackled with instructions: "Patient in Bay 3 requires immediate attention." Wristbands and badges fluttered as nurses and doctors rushed to the call. 

By the window, a waiting chair was occupied by a patient’s relative, visibly agitated. "Why is it taking so long?" they complained, their voice echoing through the sterile hallway. The register of clinical urgency was strict: "Bay 5: Chest pain, potential MI," the intercom announced, followed by another page: "Bay 8: Severe allergic reaction, needs epinephrine now."

The nurse at the desk checked her watch, then dialed a number on the phone. "This way, please," she directed a new arrival, her voice calm yet firm. The gurney moved down the corridor, the patient’s movements barely perceptible under the sheet. The curtain drew back, and the doctor entered, his face grave. The monitor beside the patient flickered with vital signs, and the nurse applied fresh adhesive strips to the wristband, updating it with the latest information.
